Letter
Age-Induced Reduction in Human Lipolysis:
A Potential Role for Adipocyte
Noradrenaline Degradation
Hui Gao,1 Peter Arner,2 Gallic Beauchef,3 Christelle Gue´ re´ ,3 Katell Vie,3 Ingrid Dahlman,2 Niklas Mejhert,2,4
and Mikael Ryde´ n2,4,*
1Department of Biosciences and Nutrition (H2), Karolinska Institutet, Huddinge 141 83, Sweden
2Department of Medicine (H7), Karolinska Institutet, Karolinska University Hospital, Huddinge, 141 86 Stockholm, Sweden
3CLARINS Laboratoires, 95300 Pontoise, France
4These authors contributed equally
*Correspondence: mikael.ryden@ki.se
https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cmet.2020.06.007
Adipocyte lipolysis is an enzymatically
regulated process that hydrolyzes stored
triacylglycerols into free fatty acids and
glycerol ( Arner et al., 2018 ). It is primarily
stimulated by catecholamines (noradren-
aline and adrenaline) acting through
beta-adrenoceptors. Ligand binding to
these receptors results in increased intra-
cellular levels of cyclic AMP (cAMP),
which in turn stimulates protein kinase A
and lipase activity. Attenuated catechol-
amine-induced lipolysis negatively im-
pacts lipid turnover, promotes white adi-
pose tissue (WAT) accumulation,
reduces the ability to withstand starva-
tion, and may also affect the ability to
maintain core body temperature ( Arner
et al., 2018 ; Ryde´ n et al., 2020 ; Toth and
Tchernof, 2000 ). Importantly, these are
all features commonly observed with ag-
ing ( Lo¨ nnqvist et al., 1990 ; Ryde´ n
et al., 2020 ).
The molecular mechanisms underlying
attenuated adipocyte lipolysis in aging
have remained elusive. It was therefore
with great interest that we read the recent
work by Camell et al. (2017, 2019) in which
they studied the role of the immune sys-
tem in age-related changes in lipolysis.
Brieﬂy, the authors showed that aging in-
duces the expression of an enzyme,
monoamine oxidase A (MAOA), which ca-
tabolizes the ﬁrst step in catecholamine
degradation ( Camell et al., 2017 ). This
occurs speciﬁcally in adipose tissue mac-
rophages (ATMs) and leads to lower cate-
cholamine levels in the WAT microenvi-
ronment, which thereby reduces
lipolysis. Subsequently, the same group
suggested that a speciﬁc B cell popula-
tion in WAT may contribute to these age-
related changes in part through crosstalk
with ATMs (Camell et al., 2019). All results
were based on studies in mice and the
translational relevance for humans is un-
clear given that there are important quali-
tative species differences in lipolysis
regulation ( Arner et al., 2018 ). We there-
fore aimed to elucidate whether similar
mechanisms operate in human WAT.
In a longitudinal study ( Arner et al.,
2018)( clinicaltrials.gov, NCT02227043),
we followed a cohort of 25 weight-stable
women for 13 ± 0.8 years (clinical charac-
teristics detailed in Table S1). At baseline,
the participants were on average middle-
aged and had a body mass index (BMI)
in the obese range ( Figures S1 A and
S1B). Three subjects had fasting plasma
glucose between 6.1 and 6.9 mM
(impaired fasting glucose, IFG) while the
rest were otherwise healthy. None re-
ported any regular medication and all
were pre-menopausal. At follow-up, the
average BMI of the cohort was not signif-
icantly altered ( Figure S1B). Eight women
displayed IFG and three had developed
type 2 diabetes (two of which treated
with metformin). Seventeen had under-
gone menopause. Abdominal subcutane-
ous WAT biopsies were obtained and
functionally characterized at the ﬁrst and
second clinical examinations. In accor-
dance with Camell et al. (2017), WAT lipol-
ysis was reduced over time ( Figure S1C).
To link this to changes in gene expression,
microarrays were performed and
analyzed using a linear model based on
pairwise comparisons adjusting for BMI.
This identiﬁed 907 and 119 genes to be
up- or downregulated, respectively,
comparing the second with the ﬁrst visit.
The differentially expressed genes were
enriched in pathways that grouped into
four main clusters, monoamine degrada-
tion, signaling and inﬂammation, senes-
cence and DNA repair, and mitochondrial
metabolism, as well as two individual
pathways, adipogenesis and protein turn-
over (Figure S1D). Notably, several of the
genes in the monoamine degradation
cluster, e.g., MAOA and ALDH2, were
previously reported to be regulated by
age in mice ( Camell et al., 2017 ).
Camell et al. attributed increased
monoamine degradation primarily to
ATMs ( Camell et al., 2017 ). Given that
our analyses were based on intact WAT,
we dissected the main cell contributor of
the age-regulated genes by overlapping
our results with transcriptomic data from
different cell types of human WAT (Acosta
et al., 2017 ). In comparison with most
other clusters, this revealed that genes
encoding monoamine degradation en-
zymes were highly expressed in mature
adipocytes and to a lesser degree in
adipocyte progenitors, but not in ATMs
(including M1 and M2-macrophages) or
T cells ( Figures S1 E and S1F). The fat
cell-speciﬁc expression was validated by
qPCR ( Figure S1 G). Our data therefore
suggest that in contrast to mice, aging pri-
marily affects the expression of mono-
amine degradation in human adipocytes.
To test this, we isolated mature adipo-
cytes and determined the lipolytic effect
of noradrenaline ex vivo at the ﬁrst and
second examination. As a control, we
used the cAMP analog dibuturyl cAMP
(dcAMP), which acts at the post-receptor
level and is therefore not affected by
changes in catecholamine degradation.
Using noradrenaline, we observed a sig-
niﬁcant reduction in lipolysis with age
(Figure S1H, left panel) and similar effects

were observed at submaximal concentra-
tions (1 3 10/C08 mol/L) corresponding to
circulating levels of noradrenaline (graph
not shown). In contrast, with dcAMP the
pro-lipolytic effects were similar at both
visits ( Figure S1 H, right panel), indicating
that the noradrenaline results were not
due to a generalized impairment of the
lipolytic machinery downstream of recep-
tor activation. In support of this, we
observed no age-induced alterations in
the enrichment of the lipolysis pathway
(including all genes encoding adrenocep-
tors and postreceptor regulators;
Figure S1I).
To further substantiate a relationship
between catecholamine degradation and
age-related alterations in noradrenaline-
stimulated lipolysis, we analyzed the as-
sociation between changes in gene
expression and lipolysis over time. This
showed that the increase in MAOA
mRNA levels with age was inversely
correlated with the decrease in noradren-
aline-stimulated lipolysis (Figure S1J). The
observed relationship also remained sta-
tistically signiﬁcant after correction for
menopause status (by ANOVA or t test;
data not shown).
Our longitudinal analyses were per-
formed in subcutaneous WAT from
women, and we cannot exclude that there
may be depot and/or gender-speciﬁc dif-
ferences in lipolysis regulation with age.
Unfortunately, human visceral WAT
cannot be studied prospectively. More-
over, MAOA in visceral WAT may display
a different cell expression distribution,
e.g., in speciﬁc macrophages. We ad-
dressed the latter by analyzing published
single-cell data from the stromal-vascular
fraction of human subcutaneous and
visceral WAT ( Vijay et al., 2020 ). This
demonstrated that MAOA in both depots
was not expressed in immune cells (graph
not shown). Furthermore, data from the
FANTOM5 expression atlas ( Forrest
et al., 2014 ), encompassing RNA
sequencing data from hundreds of human
and murine tissues and cell types,
conﬁrmed that MAOA was signiﬁcantly
enriched only in mature fat cells while
Maoa displayed a much broader cellular
distribution and was expressed in macro-
phages, adipocytes, and neurons
(Figure S1 K). Altogether, these data sup-
port the notion of a species-speciﬁc dif-
ference in MAOA expression in WAT, irre-
spective of depot.
In summary, human adipocyte lipolysis
induced by the endogenous catechol-
amine noradrenaline is reduced by aging,
but the lipolysis signaling pathway per se
appears intact. Instead, our results sug-
gest that a selective increase in multiple
genes of monoamine catabolism (all pre-
dominantly expressed in mature adipo-
cytes) underlie the observed changes
(Figure S1L). In addition to key degrading
enzymes, this includes the organic cation
transporter OCT3 (encoded by SLC22A3),
which transports noradrenaline across
the cell membrane and thereby impacts
catecholamine clearance and lipolysis in
WAT in vivo (Song et al., 2019 ). Thus,
our results largely support the data by
Camell et al. on the age-related role of
monoamine catabolism in WAT. However,
when extending these ﬁndings to hu-
mans, mature adipocytes, not ATMs,
appear to be the main contributors to
the age-induced effects on WAT lipid
mobilization.

ous and visceral WAT depots reported in the orig-
inal publication ( Vijay et al., 2020 ). The study was
supported by grants from the Swedish Research

sortium NNF15SA0018346), the Stockholm
County Council, CIMED, the Strategic Research
Program in Diabetes at Karolinska Institutet, the
Swedish Diabetes Foundation, and the Swedish
Society of Medicine.
